title: The Galton board
hook: Beads bounce at random through pegs, yet always pile up into the same bell curve.
peek: Drop a few thousand beads through rows of pegs and each one takes a path of pure chance. Yet together they settle into a smooth bell-shaped heap, every time. Francis Galton built the board in the 1870s to show how order comes out of randomness.
lede: A Galton board is an upright board studded with staggered rows of pegs, with a row of slots at the bottom. Each bead that falls hits a peg and goes left or right, like a coin toss, again and again. No single bead can be predicted. But pour in thousands and the slots fill into the same bell-shaped curve, tallest in the middle.

bullets.text: The Victorian scientist Francis Galton built his board in the 1870s and called it a quincunx, after the five-dot pattern on a die that the pegs repeat. He used it in lectures and in his 1889 book Natural Inheritance.

The number of routes to each slot follows Pascal's triangle. A bead needs a near-even mix of lefts and rights to land in the middle, and there are far more ways to do that than to go all left or all right.

The board is a working model of one of the great results in statistics: add up many small random nudges and the total tends towards a bell curve. It is a large part of why heights, measurement errors and exam marks often look bell-shaped.

Galton also described a board with a second stage below the first, to show that a bell curve made of many smaller bell curves is still a bell curve. He was using it to think about how traits pass from parents to children.
